assumptionSets.name: FY27 Baseline
assumptionSets.notes: Phase 3 addendum: choice-model parameters (switching cost, expansion propensity, sales-cycle lognormals, per-process importance weights, brand bias) layered onto the Phase 2 flow parameters of the same assumption set.

parameters.rationale: Anchors the utility scale: at the default price sensitivity of 1.0, $5,000 of monthly subscription costs exactly one unit of utility - and one unit of utility is what a maximum-importance process gains going from not-playing to gold. $5,000/month is the middle of this market's list prices ($4,000 boutique to $8,000 enterprise for the suite), i.e. a firm will trade roughly the whole platform price for market-leading capability on the single process it cares most about. The engine default of 1,000 made the price term 4-8 utility units against a total coverage term of at most ~2.5, so no offer could ever beat the outside option and 84% of deals ended in no-decision regardless of what we shipped.

The outside option is the origin of the utility scale: 'keep the status quo' scores zero, and every candidate is measured as coverage minus price relative to it. Asserted explicitly rather than left to the default so the anchor is visible with its provenance. With price-scale 5,000 this puts baseline no-decision at roughly one evaluated opportunity in six.

Baseline switching friction: moving off an incumbent costs about 0.35 utility units, i.e. $1,750/month-equivalent of disruption on the price scale - roughly a third of a mid-market monthly subscription.

Puts a need's monthly workaround cost on exactly the same utility scale as the price term: 1 / choice.price-scale (5,000), so a dollar of workaround cost and a dollar of subscription hurt equally. A $600/month filing workaround is then worth 0.12 utility units.
Baseline probability an opportunity's scope expands mid-cycle when we hold a coverage advantage on adjacent processes.
